title: DARPA SyNAPSE → IBM TrueNorth chip
summary: DARPA's SyNAPSE program, started in 2008, paid outside performers including IBM and university partners to build low-power, brain-inspired neuromorphic chips; DARPA did not run the hardware work itself, so this is a contracted research program whose result stayed with the contractor rather than a government function handed over after it ended. In August 2014 DARPA announced a one-million-neuron chip designed by IBM under SyNAPSE, which IBM's team named TrueNorth and described in Science; trade press reported DARPA had invested $53 million in the project. IBM later sold a TrueNorth-based system to Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (2016). DARPA's program page says only that the program is complete, without an end date.

private.name: IBM Research (TrueNorth neurosynaptic chip)
private.outcome: The date above is the public unveiling of the chip, not IBM's founding. The chip, described by IBM in Science (Merolla et al., vol. 345, pp. 668-73), has 4,096 cores, one million neurons, 256 million synapses and 5.4 billion transistors, built on Samsung's 28nm process. The program end date used here is the DARPA announcement of this final chip milestone; DARPA's archived program page gives no end date. In 2016 Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory contracted for a 16-chip TrueNorth system for NNSA research.

links.claim: DARPA announced on 7 August 2014 that a chip with one million electronic neurons and more than 250 million synapses, designed by IBM researchers in San Jose, had been developed under its SyNAPSE program, naming defense uses such as mobile robots and remote sensors.

links.claim: InformationWeek reported in August 2014 that DARPA had invested $53 million in IBM's SyNAPSE project to date, funding it since 2008; IBM's lead researcher wrote that DARPA's mandate, metrics and investment were vital to the chip.

claims.claim: IBM's TrueNorth chip was paid for by DARPA.
claims.explanation: DARPA states the chip was developed under its SyNAPSE program and IBM's lead researcher calls DARPA's investment vital; trade press put DARPA's investment at $53 million. The records opened do not show what IBM itself spent, so it cannot be said DARPA paid the whole cost.
